title: No clock unless speed counts
statement: Put a clock on a test only when working against time is part of what it measures; on an untimed test a clock changes what is measured.
detail: A reading assessment dropped timed sections because the test it mirrors is an untimed power test, where a clock changes the construct and rewards the rapid guessing that test penalizes (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/00_BRAINLIFT.md`). An audit of a reading course's positions lists 'comprehension is untimed; speed is a different construct' as borrowed from reading research, but names no study for its claim that time pressure triples the on-screen accuracy penalty (`grade3-reading/artifacts/team-direction-2026-09-09/research/02-current-brainlift-spov-audit.md`). A clock fits, for example, when a test rehearses a timed exam.
against: One course plan asks for a timer on a mock exam so that it mirrors the timed AP exam, which is why the rule allows a clock when a test rehearses a timed exam; that plan is not cited because its file's path carries a person's name.

evidence.quote: | Timed sections | MAP is an untimed power test; a clock changes the construct and rewards the rapid-guessing MAP penalizes |
Comprehension is untimed; speed is a different construct; time-pressure triples the on-screen accuracy penalty.
The gap appears only for expository text, grows under time pressure, and digital natives show no advantage.
Remove time pressure and ask for a self-check before showing answers.
| Timing | Untimed — power test, not speed test | NWEA published guidance [NWEA-VERIFIED] |
